alternative: A worker pool (Node worker_threads or browser Web Workers, pre-warmed and message-driven) for CPU-bound work; async/await with Promise.all for I/O-bound fan-out.
idiom_name: none in-language; a Worker pool (worker_threads / Web Workers) is the substitute
implementation_notes: JavaScript's execution model is one event loop with no in-process threads, so CPU-bound fork/join cannot be expressed with language primitives: the closest async idiom, Promise.all over subtasks, interleaves I/O but does not run JavaScript in parallel. The substitute is a pool of Worker threads (Node worker_threads, browser Web Workers): "fork" posts a data slice to a worker and "join" collects results through message events or promises. There is no work stealing and no stdlib pool - the pool is hand-built (the Node docs say to use one and point at AsyncResource for the correlation), and data crosses by structured clone or transfer rather than shared memory. Use it for CPU-heavy recursion; keep async/await + Promise.all for I/O-bound fan-out, where parallelism is not the goal.
pitfalls: Spawning a Worker per subtask costs far more than the task returns; only a pre-warmed, reused pool pays off, and the standard library ships none.
Messages are structured-cloned (or transferred, which neuters the sender's buffer): large slices are copied, and shared mutation requires SharedArrayBuffer plus Atomics.
Errors, cancellation and stack traces do not cross the worker boundary: a crashed worker must be replaced by the pool, and each task needs its own completion protocol.
